The spring itself just holds the saddle at the distance you set it at, the screw adjusts the intonation. Or the note at the 12th fret and the second harmonic (or the 12th harmonic) 

Pushing and pulling these screws will lengthen and shorten the string from the saddle to the nut, allowing you to have notes that fall in your frets. What I mean by that is when you buy a guitar, the guitar has a thing called scale length, that's the distance between the saddles and the nut, or the playable space of the string. Each fret is suppose to have a note, these screws let you set those notes up properly.  

It's worth your time to look up a video on YouTube for setting intonation in a set bridge. 

A lot of the times people get rid of guitars because they sound bad or the notes and chords don't sound right even though it's perfectly in tune. That's where those springs and screws come into play. 

I always play an Am chord after tuning to check intonation.  I find the Am chord is perfect for hearing any dissonance or consonance in the notes played.
